extracted.intended_audience: mathematics teachers and students (classroom; puzzle/contest/problem-solving context)
extracted.subtask_description: Analyze and solve puzzles about coloring a 10x10 board into rectangular regions by suits, determining freebies, minimal guesses to complete the board, enumerating configuration classes, and counting distinct boards under symmetry. Solutions use geometric partitioning, case analysis, and combinatorial counting.

rubrics_metrics.name: determine_minimal_n_for_completion
rubrics_metrics.description: Determine the values of n such that knowing a specific n squares still does not complete the board, but knowing an (n+1)st square allows you to complete the board.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Use sample boards to explain. (Problem statement: 'Determine the values of n such that knowing a speciﬁc n squares still does not complete the board, but knowing an .n C 1/st square allows you to complete the board. Use sample boards to explain.')

rubrics_metrics.name: identify_freebies (forced squares)
rubrics_metrics.description: Locate 'freebies' — squares whose suits can be deduced without guessing because of rectangular borders and previously known suits.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Identify rectangles defined by given vertices whose interior squares become forced. Examples: 'There are 10 freebies. They are in the rectangle with vertices at (6,3), (6,6), (4,6), and (4,3).' and other enumerated rectangles in solution examples.

rubrics_metrics.name: good_guess_strategy
rubrics_metrics.description: Choose guesses that have the potential to reveal many freebies or that resolve borders between suits.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: A good guess can reveal many freebies. Students should look for borders between suits or guess squares that have more possibilities for their suits. Example guidance: 'A good guess has the potential to reveal many freebies. ... students might look for borders between suits or guess squares that have more possibilities for their suits.'

rubrics_metrics.name: corner_color_analysis_to_detect_traversing_borders
rubrics_metrics.description: Analyze the four corner colors: if any adjacent corner pair is the same color, a rectangle will extend from one edge to the opposite edge creating a border that traverses the board.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Use the corners to infer the existence of a vertical or horizontal border that traverses the entire board. (From solution: 'Consider the four corners of the board. If any adjacent pair is the same color, then one of the four rectangles would extend from one edge of the board to the opposite edge.')

rubrics_metrics.name: partition_unit_square_and_case_ordering
rubrics_metrics.description: Model the board as a unit square partitioned into four rectangles and analyze by ordering the x and y coordinates of interior rectangle vertices (a, b, c, d) to enumerate cases.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Denote the four rectangular regions as A, B, C, and D and their interior vertices a,b,c,d with coordinates; deduce which rectangles must share vertical/horizontal borders and enumerate the possible orderings of x and y values (nine ways mentioned). Use symmetry to eliminate impossible cases where rectangles would be uncolored or doubly colored. (Example: 'We find it useful to solve this problem by viewing the board as a unit square, partitioned into four rectangles... There are nine ways in which the x and y values of the vertices can be ordered.')

rubrics_metrics.name: use_symmetry_and_case_elimination
rubrics_metrics.description: Exploit symmetry to reduce casework and eliminate configurations that lead to contradictions (e.g., uncolored rectangle or double-colored rectangle).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Many cases are ruled out by symmetry or because they would create an uncolored rectangle or a rectangle colored twice. (Examples: 'In case 1a/... this case cannot occur. Due to symmetry, case 3c/ cannot occur for the same reason.'; 'In case 1c/... this case cannot occur.')

rubrics_metrics.name: classification_by_sequential_division_decision_tree
rubrics_metrics.description: Enumerate configuration classes by building a decision tree of sequential horizontal/vertical divisions (first action identified by h/v), counting possibilities for 3, 2, or 1 traversing parallel line segments.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Because an initial horizontal or vertical division is rotationally equivalent, identify first action as h or v. For 3 parallel segments there is one configuration; for 2 there are two; for 1 there are multiple terminal configurations (d,e,f). Use the decision tree (Figure 8) to list terminal nodes and classes. Note: the decision-tree method is used to enumerate configuration classes and terminal nodes.

rubrics_metrics.name: recognize_limitations_of_decision_tree_method
rubrics_metrics.description: Be aware that sequential division (decision tree) does not generate all ways to divide the square into rectangles; some divisions have no border traversing the entire board and thus aren't produced by the tree.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Provide counterexamples to show the method is not exhaustive (example: 'the division of the 10x10 square into rectangles in Figure 7a cannot be generated by extending the decision tree approach... because no border traverses the entire length of the 10x10 board while the first line drawn in the decision tree approach traverses the entire board').

rubrics_metrics.name: count_configuration_classes_and_apply_symmetry
rubrics_metrics.description: Count distinct configuration classes of rectangle partitions, identifying equivalences under rotation and listing the number of unique terminal nodes.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: There are 6 configuration classes; some boards (e.g., two denoted by c/) are equivalent under rotation while other terminal nodes are unique. Use rotational equivalence to reduce counts. (From solution: 'There are 6 conﬁguration classes. The 2 boards denoted by c/ in Figure 8 are equivalent.')

rubrics_metrics.name: count_boards_by_border_choices_and_suit_allocations
rubrics_metrics.description: Count the number of distinct boards in a configuration class by counting choices of horizontal/vertical borders and allocating suits to regions, incorporating symmetry factors.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: For a given configuration class, count possible choices of border lines (e.g., choose from 9 possible horizontal borders etc.), multiply by suit allocations (4^k for k regions), and account for rotation equivalence between horizontal and vertical classes. The solutions show enumerative formulas combining these factors. (Example language: 'There are ways to choose these horizontal borders. Suits in each of these boards can be allocated in 4^? ways. And, because horizontal and vertical borders are in the same conﬁguration class under rotation, the total number of boards in this conﬁguration class is ...')
